verdict.text:
Track 1 cannot be evaluated on this run. Every slot carries `support_gold_missing = 0` and every `gold_slots` entry is an empty string, so there were no adjudicated gold labels to score against. The zeros across precision, recall and F1 — and the 0.9 "agreement rate" — are artifacts of absent gold, not model behaviour. The requirements in this set have evidently not been adjudicated yet. Nothing about fabrication or missing-slot flagging can be concluded here, in either direction.

What the LLM's own output still shows is its flagging *tendency*: it declared scope missing 7 times out of 30 and collapsed into near-total placeholders on 83-Signal and 1504-Signal, both of which are effectively contentless source texts ("No description provided", "how about we edit this one too? or just delete it"). That is arguably the right instinct, and the humans on 83-Signal largely agreed. Conversely, on 496-Signal the model produced a confident "the System shall enable the ability to change maximum size of MMS" while all three annotators marked most slots missing — the fabrication pattern the study is designed to catch. 1283-Signal is the clearest instance: the model invented a rationale clause ("based on adoption from competing platforms like Go SMS PRO") and inverted the actor, making the User request the System, where all three humans wrote the App as actor. 801-Signal both invented a condition absent from the source and leaked a literal `<NON_ATOMIC>` token into the output.

The similarity gap (seq_ratio 0.42 against a human ceiling of 0.58; Jaccard 0.26 against 0.47) is real but should be read cautiously. Human-human variance is enormous (std 0.31, min 0.0), the 89 pairs are not independent, and a substantial share of the gap is lexical convention rather than comprehension: humans consistently write "For all users, ... the App must ...", while zsl writes "For <MISSING_SCOPE>, the System shall ...". That mismatch penalises every requirement uniformly. Until the scope/actor lexicon is pinned in the prompt, this number understates semantic agreement by an unknown amount, and cross-strategy comparisons built on it are unsafe.

Paska's 73% pass rate is the most interpretable figure, though with only 8 failures no smell type is distinguishable from another. The three "Not requirement" hits (83, 1504, 6077-Signal) are the degenerate placeholder outputs and are arguably correct refusals rather than defects. The single non-atomic hit on 6457-
